interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the field hold steady and the speed dip only slightly, as the back-emf falls a little and the armature current rises, when you drag the load up.
interactive.title: Load it, weaken the field
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Nine screens, with Back and Continue. One picture to play with, three quick choices and a card to keep. No marks and no timers.

Assume one motor on every screen: a DC shunt motor rated 600 V and 2000 rpm, with a 0.07 Ω armature and an 80 Ω field, drawing 353 A at rated load.[^1] It is a worked example, not a nameplate. Every other figure is worked from it, or is a labelled example.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: "A DC motor is switched straight onto its supply. Before it starts to turn, what sets the current it draws?" Three choices, in this order: "Its back-emf, which opposes the supply"; "Only the resistance of its armature circuit"; "The inductance of its windings, as on AC". Right, the second: "Still there. A motor makes back-emf only as it turns, so at standstill there is none. Only the resistance limits the current. Take a motor with a 0.07 Ω armature on 600 V. Switched straight on, it would take 600 ÷ 0.07 = 8571 A. That is why it starts through a starter." Wrong, the first: "Back-emf comes from turning. At standstill there is none, so it cannot hold the current back yet." Wrong, the third: "Inductance only slows how fast the current rises. At standstill, once it settles, only resistance limits a DC current." After a wrong choice, the right answer and its reason, then on to screen 2. No skip button.

Screen 2, How it works. A still drawing: a DC supply labelled "600 V" with two branches across it, side by side. On the left, the field winding with a field rheostat in series, labelled "shunt field". On the right, the armature between its brushes. An arrow from the supply splits into "field current" and "armature current". A curved arrow shows the armature turning, and a label "back-emf" points against the supply. The words beside it: "The field winding is wired across the supply, beside the armature. So its current and its flux stay steady whatever the load. Load the motor and it slows a little. Its back-emf falls, so more armature current flows. More current gives more torque. It settles where the torque matches the load, a little slower than before. Unlike a series motor's field, this one does not follow the load. So the speed hardly moves." Shunt field is the key term, marked in amber.

Screen 3, Load it, weaken the field: the picture to play with. At the top, screen 2's circuit redrawn small, with an arrow on the field rheostat and "V = 600 V" beside the supply's cell. Beside the field winding, a bar for its flux, labelled with the field current in amperes. Next, two bars. Back-emf, on a scale of 0 to 600 V. Armature drop, Ia × Ra, on a scale of 0 to 60 V, labelled "drawn 10 times bigger". Then a plot: speed in rpm, 0 to 3600, against load, 0 to 100% of rated torque. The speed line for the present field setting is drawn in full, with a dot at the load slider's value. A band above 2500 rpm is shaded red and labelled "example limit, not a maker's". Then one row of three readouts: Armature current, A. Back-emf, V. Speed, rpm. The armature current turns red above its rated 345.5 A. The speed turns red above 2500 rpm. On a phone these sit one under another. On a laptop the plot sits beside the circuit.

The controls. Load: a slider from 0 to 100% of rated torque in steps of 10. It starts at 0, running light. Field rheostat: a slider from 0 to 50 Ω in steps of 10. It starts at 0, full field. Field circuit: a switch, Connected or Open. It starts on Connected.

The rule it works out is for a simplified shunt motor. Flux follows field current. There is no saturation, no armature reaction and no brush drop.
Field current If = 600 ÷ (80 + rheostat). Flux = If ÷ 7.5, so 1.00 at full field.
Armature current Ia = (17.3 + 328.2 × load) ÷ flux, with load as a fraction of rated. 17.3 A is an example no-load current, 5% of rated. It only covers the motor's own friction and iron losses. 328.2 A is the rest of the rated 345.5 A. Torque goes with flux × Ia. So dividing by the flux keeps the torque matched to the load.
Back-emf E = 600 − Ia × 0.07.
Speed = 2000 × (E ÷ 575.8) ÷ flux. Back-emf goes with flux × speed, and is 575.8 V at 2000 rpm on full field.

Under the readouts, a box shows the working for the present setting only. Each line uses the rounded figures before it. At any other setting the box names the settings that have working. With the field open the box is hidden.
Rated load, full field: If = 600 ÷ 80 = 7.5 A. Ia = 353 − 7.5 = 345.5 A. Drop = 345.5 × 0.07 = 24.2 V. E = 600 − 24.2 = 575.8 V. Speed 2000 rpm.
No load, full field: Ia = 17.3 A. That is an example, 5% of 345.5 A. Drop = 17.3 × 0.07 = 1.2 V. E = 600 − 1.2 = 598.8 V. Speed = 2000 × 598.8 ÷ 575.8 = 2080 rpm.
Half load, full field: the load's share is half of 345.5 − 17.3 = 328.2 A, so 164.1 A. Ia = 17.3 + 164.1 = 181.4 A. Drop = 181.4 × 0.07 = 12.7 V. E = 587.3 V. Speed = 2000 × 587.3 ÷ 575.8 = 2040 rpm.
Rheostat 20 Ω, rated load: If = 600 ÷ 100 = 6.0 A. Flux = 6.0 ÷ 7.5 = 0.80. Ia = 345.5 ÷ 0.80 = 431.9 A, above rated. Drop = 431.9 × 0.07 = 30.2 V. E = 600 − 30.2 = 569.8 V. Speed = 2000 × 569.8 ÷ (575.8 × 0.80) = 2000 × 569.8 ÷ 460.64 = 2474 rpm.
Rheostat 20 Ω, no load: Ia = 17.3 ÷ 0.80 = 21.6 A. Drop = 21.6 × 0.07 = 1.5 V. E = 598.5 V. Speed = 2000 × 598.5 ÷ 460.64, about 2600 rpm, past the example limit.

Field open. The flux bar drops to a sliver, labelled "residual magnetism only". The picture prints no figures here. A note under the circuit says how fast it goes depends on the load and on how much magnetism the iron keeps, and that the 30% load split is an example. On a load of 30% or less, the speed dot climbs from where it was into the red band near the top, leaving a trail, labelled "Runs away". On a heavier load the armature current readout shows "far above rated" in red, labelled "Its protection should trip it". Switch back to Connected and the picture returns to the rule above.

The words on the screen, above the picture: "Assume this 600 V motor: 0.07 Ω armature and 80 Ω field. At rated load it runs at 2000 rpm and draws 353 A from the supply. The supply covers the back-emf and the armature drop: V = E + Ia Ra. Back-emf goes with flux × speed. Torque goes with flux × Ia. The no-load current and the 2500 rpm limit are examples." The prompt above the picture: "Drag the load up. Then add field resistance. Then open the field." Read: From no load to rated load the field current stays at 7.5 A. The back-emf falls from 598.8 to 575.8 V. The armature current rises from 17.3 to 345.5 A. The speed dips only from 2080 to 2000 rpm. Adding 20 Ω to the field cuts its current to 6.0 A. At rated load the speed rises to 2474 rpm. The armature current rises to 431.9 A, above rated. With no load it reaches about 2600 rpm, past the example limit. With the field open on a light load, the speed runs away. Still: the field connected, the rheostat at 0 Ω and the load at 100%. The field bar is full at 7.5 A, the back-emf bar at 575.8 V and the drop bar at 24.2 V. The dot sits at 2000 rpm on a nearly flat line, and the readouts show 345.5 A, 575.8 V and 2000 rpm.

Screen 4, Check on the cause. "A shunt motor is driving a steady load. You turn the field rheostat to add resistance. What does the speed do?" Three choices, in this order: "It rises"; "It falls"; "It holds steady". Right, the first: "Right. Less field current means less flux. The armature must spin faster to make the back-emf it needs. So the speed rises. On the picture, 20 Ω takes the rated-load speed from 2000 to 2474 rpm. That is called field weakening." Wrong, the second: "That is what resistance in the armature circuit does. In the field circuit it weakens the flux. A weaker field must spin faster, so the speed rises." Wrong, the third: "The load is the same, but the flux is not. Less flux needs more speed for the same back-emf. So the speed rises." After a wrong choice, the right answer and its reason.

Screen 5, How it behaves. A still drawing: screen 3's speed line at full field, nearly flat from 2080 rpm at no load to 2000 rpm at rated load, labelled "sketch from the simplified rule". Rows, each with a label.

Speed: "Nearly constant.[^10] Its speed regulation is (no-load − full-load speed) ÷ full-load speed.[^2] Here (2080 − 2000) ÷ 2000 = 4.0%. Quoted figures run from about 5 to 10%.[^7] Some sheets give 10 to 20%.[^3] Use the maker's figure."

Starting torque: "Lower than a series motor's, as its field does not grow with the current.[^5] Typically about 250%, as the starter's current limit allows.[^4]"

Speed control: "Base speed is the nameplate speed at full field and full armature volts. Below it, lower the armature volts. Above it, weaken the field.[^12]"

Reversing: "Swap the armature or the field leads, not both.[^13]"

Speed regulation is the key term, marked in amber.

Screen 6, Where it is used, and its limits. A still drawing: the motor driving a conveyor, with a thyristor drive feeding its armature. Rows.

Used for: "Pumps, fans, blowers, conveyors, machine tools and printing. Anywhere the speed must hold steady as the load changes."

Unloaded: "Safe with no load at full field, as long as the field stays connected. Losing the load is not the danger it is for a series motor."

Drive: "It pairs well with a thyristor drive, which sets the armature voltage. Many plants have moved to AC motors on VSDs.[^24] Brush and commutator upkeep is a big reason.[^25]"

Limits: "Brushes and commutator need regular care. Field weakening must not take it past the nameplate's maximum safe speed.[^6] A weakened field can overspeed at light load."

Screen 7, Faults and tests. A still drawing: the isolator open with a lock and tag on it, a megger from the windings to frame, an ohmmeter across the field leads, and the brushes on the commutator. Rows.

Safety first: "Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch it."

Field open: "On a light load it can run away. Loss-of-field protection guards against it."

Starting: "Start at full field, with the rheostat at its slow-speed position."

Starter: "A three-point starter's no-volt coil works like the DOL's latch. Lose the supply and its handle drops to off. The coil carries the field current, so an open field drops it too."

Sparking: "Look for worn brushes, a rough commutator or an armature fault."

Tests: "Megger the windings to frame. Measure the armature and field resistance. An open field reads open circuit."

Screen 8, Find the fault. "A shunt motor drives a conveyor that is running almost empty. It has run at a steady speed for years. Today it races until its protection trips. What is the most likely fault?" Three choices, in this order: "The belt came off, so it lost its load"; "The shunt field circuit has gone open"; "The brushes have worn down". Right, the second: "Right. With the field open, only residual magnetism is left. The armature must spin far faster to make its back-emf. On a light load it runs away. Isolate and prove dead. Then test the field winding, its rheostat and its connections for an open circuit." Wrong, the first: "That is the series motor's trap. A shunt motor's field stays steady with no load. Running light at full field, it goes only a little faster." Wrong, the third: "Worn brushes cause sparking and poor contact. They make a motor weak or slow, not race." After a wrong choice, the right answer and its reason.

Screen 9, Keep this: the summary card, without the worked figures. Then Finish the lesson.

Every figure on these screens is a control, worked from a rule shown, a cited value or a labelled example. The no-load current, the 2500 rpm limit and the open-field split are examples, not a maker's.
interactive.ignores: The picture is a simplified shunt motor. Its flux follows the field current exactly, with no saturation. It ignores armature reaction. That changes the flux a little under load. On a real plain shunt motor it can stop the speed falling, or even make it rise. It also ignores brush drop and the time the motor takes to change speed. The no-load current, the red limit and the open-field split are example values, not a maker's. With the field open it prints no figures. How fast it goes depends on the load and on how much magnetism the iron keeps.

explain.text:
A DC shunt motor has its field winding wired across the supply, beside the armature. That winding is the [[shunt field]]. Its current is set by the supply voltage and its own resistance, not by the load. So the flux holds steady, and the speed stays nearly constant as the load changes.

Back-emf works as it did in the series motor. The supply has to cover it plus the drop across the armature: V = E + Ia Ra. Put a load on and the armature slows a little, so the back-emf falls. That leaves more room for Ia Ra, so more armature current flows. Torque goes with flux times current, so the torque rises. The speed settles where the torque matches the load. It does not climb back to where it was. The fall is small because the flux holds steady. Take the picture's 600 V motor, with its example no-load current. Its back-emf falls only from 598.8 V running light to 575.8 V at rated load. So the speed falls only from 2080 to 2000 rpm.

Back-emf goes with flux times speed, so speed goes with back-emf over flux. That is how the field rheostat works. Add resistance and the flux weakens. The motor must then spin faster to make its back-emf. Lose the field altogether and only residual magnetism is left. On a light load the motor can then run away. In the series motor the field followed the load. Here the load barely changes it.

How far the speed falls from no load to full load is its [[speed regulation]]. The picture's motor gives 4.0%. Quoted figures run from about 5 to 10%.[^7] Some sheets give 10 to 20%. Use the maker's figure. A plain shunt motor can even speed up a little under load. The armature's own field weakens the flux. Makers may add a light series winding to stop that. The picture is a simplified motor that leaves this out. **Its field sits across the supply and holds the flux steady. So under load a shunt motor slows only a little. It counts as a constant-speed motor.**

analogy.text: An induction motor works the same way. It slows a little under load. That slip is what makes the rotor current that carries the torque. A shunt motor does the same with back-emf. It slows a little, so the back-emf falls and more armature current flows. Both count as constant-speed motors.
analogy.breaks: An induction motor's speed is held just under its field's synchronous speed, set by the supply frequency. A shunt motor has no such fixed speed. Weaken its field and it runs faster. Lose the field and it can run away.

practice.text:
- Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch the motor or its starter.
- Before a start, set the field rheostat to full field, its slow-speed position.
- Start through the starter. Never bypass its starting resistance.
- Check that loss-of-field protection is fitted.
- Megger the windings to frame. Measure the field and armature resistance. An open field reads open circuit.
- Look at the brushes and commutator for wear, roughness and sparking.

**Rule of thumb:** speed goes with back-emf over flux. Less field means more speed. Less armature voltage means less speed.

**Worked example:** take a shunt motor rated 600 V and 2000 rpm, with a 0.07 Ω armature and an 80 Ω field. It draws 353 A at rated load.[^1] The field takes If = 600 ÷ 80 = 7.5 A. So the armature takes Ia = 353 − 7.5 = 345.5 A. Its drop is 345.5 × 0.07 = 24.2 V, so E = 600 − 24.2 = 575.8 V. Now add 20 Ω to the field at the same torque. Assume the flux follows the field current. If = 600 ÷ 100 = 6.0 A, so the flux is 0.80 of rated. Ia = 345.5 ÷ 0.80 = 431.9 A. E = 600 − 431.9 × 0.07 = 600 − 30.2 = 569.8 V. Speed = 2000 × 569.8 ÷ (575.8 × 0.80) = 2474 rpm. The armature now carries more than its rated current. So above base speed it must give less torque, at about the same power.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting it to speed back up once the current rises. It settles a little slower.
- Adding field resistance to slow it down. That weakens the field and speeds it up.
- Starting with the field weakened. That gives less starting torque and a higher speed.
- Treating it like a series motor and never running it light. It is safe unloaded at full field, while the field stays connected.
- Swapping the supply leads to reverse it. That reverses field and armature together, so it turns the same way.

summary.title: The DC shunt motor
summary.for: Work that needs a steady speed as the load changes. The field sits across the supply, so its flux holds steady. Under load the speed dips only a little.
summary.rule:
Field across the supply, so the flux holds steady.
If = V ÷ Rf
V = E + Ia Ra
Line current = Ia + If
Speed goes with E ÷ flux.
Torque goes with flux × Ia.
Speed regulation = (no-load − full-load speed) ÷ full-load speed.

Nearly constant speed. Regulation is quoted at about 5 to 10%, sometimes 10 to 20%. Use the maker's figure.
Starting torque is lower than a series motor's.
Base speed is the nameplate speed at full field and full armature volts.
Below base speed, lower the armature volts. Above it, weaken the field.
Reverse it: swap the armature or the field leads, not both.

traps.text: More field resistance means more speed, not less. Weakening the field speeds it up.
Lose the field and it can run away on a light load. Make sure loss-of-field protection is fitted.
Start at full field, with the rheostat at its slow-speed position. Start through the starter's resistance.
It does not speed back up after a load goes on. It usually settles a little slower. That fall is its speed regulation.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead. Then megger to frame, measure field and armature resistance, and check the brushes and commutator.
